tools.name: workflow
tools.description:
Run a JavaScript workflow script that orchestrates subagents at scale. Use this for work that fans out across many independent pieces — an audit over many files, a migration, multi-angle research, adversarial verification of findings — where you write the orchestration as a script instead of delegating turn by turn.

Script-body hooks:
- `agent(prompt, opts?): Promise<any>` — run one subagent to completion. Without `opts.schema` it resolves to the child's final text; with `opts.schema` (an object-rooted JSON Schema using ONLY type/properties/required/additionalProperties/items/enum/const/oneOf) it resolves to the validated object. Resolves `null` when the child fails (filter with `.filter(Boolean)`). Other opts: `label` (display), `phase` (progress group), and independent `provider`/`model` LLM target overrides.
- `pipeline(items, ...stages): Promise<any[]>` — run each item through the stages independently with NO barrier between stages (prefer this for multi-stage work). Each stage receives `(prev, item, index)`. A stage throw drops that ITEM to `null` and skips its remaining stages.
- `parallel(thunks): Promise<any[]>` — run zero-argument functions concurrently and await ALL of them (a barrier; use only when a stage genuinely needs every prior result together). A throwing thunk resolves to `null`.
- `phase(title)` — start a progress phase; `log(message)` — narrate progress; `args` — the tool call's `args` input, verbatim.

Misused hooks (bad arguments, unknown options, unsupported schemas, tripped caps) end the whole script instead of producing `null`. The script has no filesystem, network, timer, or Node.js APIs; the agents do the work.

script.description: The plain JavaScript body, not TypeScript and without an `export const meta` statement; top-level await is allowed. End with `return <value>`; the JSON-serializable value is this tool's result.

meta.description: The workflow identity as plain JSON, not code.

description.description: One-line description of what the workflow does.

whenToUse.description: Optional guidance on when this workflow applies.

phases.description: Optional phase declarations matched by phase() calls.

title.description: The phase title phase() calls match by exact string.

detail.description: Optional one-line description of the phase.

provider.description: Optional provider override this phase is expected to use.

model.description: Optional model override this phase is expected to use.

args.description: Optional JSON input exposed to the script as the `args` global (wrap a bare list as a field, e.g. {"files": [...]}).

run_in_background.description: Run as a background job: return a job id immediately instead of waiting; the return value arrives with the completion notice.

Implement parse_duration.

Let's think spec. We'll parse text, strip whitespace. If empty raise ValueError.

Allow components separated by optional single spaces (maybe multiple spaces?). "Components may be separated by single spaces". We'll allow any whitespace maybe.

Approach:

- Strip leading/trailing whitespace.
- If text is empty: raise.
- If text is just digits (maybe with optional +/-?). Must be non-negative integer. So if only digits, return int.

- Else we need to parse series of <int><unit> where unit is one of d,h,m,s case-insensitive.

- The units must be in decreasing order d, h, m, s and each at most once.

- Also allow spaces between components.

Implementation: iterate through tokens. Could use regex: pattern r'(?i)^\s*(\d+[dhms])(?:\s*\d+[dhms])*\s*$' but need order enforcement.

Simpler: split by whitespace into parts = text.split() (splits on any whitespace). But also need to support no spaces (like "1h30m") where units combine. So need to parse character by character.

We can scan string:

Initialize index 0, last_unit_index = -1 (order index). total_seconds = 0. Use dict mapping unit->seconds.

allowed_units = {'d':0, 'h':1, 'm':2, 's':3} where smaller index bigger unit? Actually decreasing order d(0) > h(1) > m(2) > s(3). So we ensure each unit's index >= last_unit_index (since we want decreasing order, unit indices should increase). Actually if we parse left to right, units should be decreasing: d before h before m before s. So the sequence's indices should be non-decreasing (0,1,2,3). So we can check that unit_index >= last_index else invalid.

Also each unit only once, so track visited set.

Parsing algorithm:

While i < len(text):
- If whitespace: i++ continue
- Parse number: must have at least one digit. Collect digits. If none -> error.
- Then look for optional unit char: if i < len and char is alphabetic. If char is letter, interpret as unit; else, if no unit (e.g., at end after digits with no unit) -> this is the bare integer case only allowed if it's the only component and no other components. Actually spec: "A bare integer with no unit is interpreted as seconds: "120" ->120 . Also "0" valid." So if we encounter digits and next char is not a unit (or end), we treat as seconds only if we have not seen any other components (i.e., total_seconds currently zero and no previous parsed components). And ensure end of string after possible whitespace. Also ensure no other units after that.

Thus we need to detect case: after parsing number, if next char is a unit letter (d/h/m/s). If not, and we have not yet parsed any unit (i.e., no parts yet and we are at end or whitespace only), then treat it as seconds. But if after that there are other components, invalid.

Simplify: First try to split by whitespace into tokens, but tokens like "1h30m" will be a single token containing multiple components. So need to parse each token further.

Alternative: Use regex to find all occurrences of number+unit (case-insensitive). Use re.finditer(r'(\d+)([dhms])', text, flags=re.I). But we need to ensure entire string is matched properly: after removing whitespace, the concatenated matches must cover entire stripped string or be a single number only.

Plan:

- stripped = text.strip()
- If empty raise ValueError.
- If stripped.isdigit(): return int(stripped)  (allow "0"? yes)
- else: verify not a digit-only with spaces etc: ambiguous.

- Use regex to find all components: pattern = r'(\d+)([dhmsDHMS])'. Use finditer.

- Build list of (num_str, unit_char, start, end). Ensure that concatenation of matched spans (ignoring whitespace) covers all characters. So we can iterate over characters, skipping whitespace, verifying each char is part of a match.

Simpler: remove spaces: compact = ''.join(stripped.split()) . This removes all whitespace.

- Then use regex fullmatch: r'(?i)^(?:\d+[dhms])+$' . This ensures only number+unit repeated.

- If not match, raise ValueError.

- Then parse the compact string sequentially: while i < len(compact): read digits, then unit char.

- Enforce order and uniqueness.

Implementation details:

- order list = ['d','h','m','s']; index map.

- visited set.

- last_index = -1

- total_seconds = 0

- loop: read digits (while i<len and isdigit). If none, error.

- Then unit = compact[i]; i+=1.

- unit_lc = unit.lower().

- if unit_lc not in index map: error.

- idx = order_index[unit_lc]; if idx < last_index: invalid order; raise.

- if unit_lc in visited: raise.

- visited add, last_index = idx.

- total_seconds += int(num) * seconds_per_unit[unit_lc].

After loop, return total_seconds.

Edge cases: "0s" -> works. "0" recognized earlier as digits.

If compact contains "0h" etc. That's okay (value zero). Should it be allowed? spec didn't forbid zero components, but order still holds.

Invalid cases: empty string, negative numbers like "-1h", decimals "1.5h", unknown units "3w", missing number "h", repeated unit.

Also "1h 30" where 30 missing unit -> our compact would become "1h30". pattern would not match because "30" no unit, causing error. Good.

Also "30m1h" order wrong; our order check will detect idx<last_index.

    # Strip whitespace and handle empty input
    stripped = text.strip()
    if not stripped:
        raise ValueError("invalid duration: empty string")

    # Bare integer interpreted as seconds
    if stripped.isdigit():
        # Leading zeros are fine, int conversion handles it
        return int(stripped)

    # Remove all whitespace for easier parsing
    compact = "".join(stripped.split())
    # Ensure the compact form consists only of <int><unit> sequences
    import re
    if not re.fullmatch(r"(?i)(?:\d+[dhms])+$", compact):
        raise ValueError(f"invalid duration: {text!r}")

    # Mapping of units to seconds and ordering index (smaller index = larger unit)
    unit_seconds = {"d": 86400, "h": 3600, "m": 60, "s": 1}
    order_index = {"d": 0, "h": 1, "m": 2, "s": 3}
    seen = set()
    last_idx = -1
    total = 0
    i = 0
    while i < len(compact):
        # parse number
        start = i
        while i < len(compact) and compact[i].isdigit():
            i += 1
        if start == i:
            raise ValueError(f"invalid duration component in {text!r}")
        number = int(compact[start:i])
        # parse unit
        if i >= len(compact):
            # No unit after number – this should have been caught by the regex unless the whole string was a bare integer, which we handled earlier.
            raise ValueError(f"missing unit in duration {text!r}")
        unit = compact[i].lower()
        i += 1
        if unit not in unit_seconds:
            raise ValueError(f"unknown unit {unit!r} in duration {text!r}")
        if unit in seen:
            raise ValueError(f"duplicate unit {unit!r} in duration {text!r}")
        idx = order_index[unit]
        if idx < last_idx:
            raise ValueError(f"units out of order in duration {text!r}")
        seen.add(unit)
        last_idx = idx
        total += number * unit_seconds[unit]
    return total
